# Changelog

Source: https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-shift-scheduling/latest/changelog.html

# Changelog

The recommendations API can now fit multiple shifts in a single API call, instead of requiring one call per shift. This is useful when several shifts have been dropped at once and you need recommendations for all of them together.

Two ordering modes are available, each as its own endpoint:

- 
`recommend-employees-batch-per-shift`returns a ranked list of employee recommendations per shift. This is useful for avoiding multiple calls to the recommendation endpoint for each shift.
- 
`recommend-employees-batch-global`returns a ranked list of employee recommendations across all shifts. This is useful for answering the question "which shift should I assign next?".

The [input metrics](https://docs.timefold.ai/user-guide/output-datasets/input-metrics) now report the number of historic shifts and historic shift groups included in the input dataset, as `historicShifts` and `historicShiftGroups` respectively.
Both fields are `null` when no historic shifts or shift groups are present.

This makes it easier to verify that the correct amount of historical data was attached to an input, especially when using rolling-window constraints that look back several weeks.

Rolling window rules can now be configured to count only the parts of shifts that overlap with the rolling window, instead of counting any whole shift that starts within the window and extend past the window.
This is configured using the new `periodShiftOverlapKind` field on rolling window rules.

```
        "rollingWindowRules": [
          {
            "id": "max4ShiftsRollingWindow",
            "rollingWindow": {
              "type": "DAILY",
              "size": 1
            },
            "minutesWorkedLimit":
            {
              "minutesWorkedMax": 300
            },
            "satisfiability": "REQUIRED",
            "periodShiftOverlapKind": "START_AND_END"
          }
        ]
```
The previous behavior of entirely counting any shift which starts in the rolling window is still supported through the `periodShiftOverlapKind` value of `START_ONLY`. Additionally, `START_ONLY` is the default behavior when this field is not specified.

The following rules support this functionality:

We have added a new demo dataset shows how to use the shift generation feature in a realistic setting that models a one-week restaurant schedule with lunch and dinner peaks, full-time and external part-time employees.

| Demand shift generation is a preview feature subject to change | 

The dataset starts with no shifts and lets Timefold generate candidate shifts from templates to cover the hourly demand, while honoring contract limits, rest periods, and split-shift pairing preferences.

The new dataset is available under key `DEMAND_SHIFT_GENERATION`.

For more information, see:

`consecutiveShiftsWorkedRules` now support a `timeOffAfterSequenceLimit` field, letting you enforce a minimum rest period between the end of one shift sequence and the start of the next.
This makes it possible to model regulations such as "after working two or more consecutive night shifts, an employee must have at least 48 hours off before their next sequence begins."

`timeOffAfterSequenceLimit` can be used alongside or independently of the existing `maximum` field.
When a `condition` is configured, the limit is only applied to sequences where that condition is met.

A new condition type `MIN_SHIFTS_WORKED_CONSECUTIVELY` has also been added, which counts only uninterrupted runs of matching shifts within a sequence, rather than the total count of matching shifts regardless of order.

`consecutiveShiftsWorkedRules` now support a new sequence definition type, `MAX_MINUTES_BETWEEN_SHIFT_END_AND_NEXT_START`.
This defines consecutive sequences based on the time between the end of one shift and the start of the next shift.

```
{
  "contracts": [
    {
      "id": "ConsecutiveShiftsContract",
      "consecutiveShiftsWorkedRules": [
        {
          "id": "MaxConsecutiveShifts",
          "maximum": 5,
          "satisfiability": "REQUIRED",
          "sequenceDefinition": {
            "type": "MAX_MINUTES_BETWEEN_SHIFT_END_AND_NEXT_START",
            "triggerLimit": 2160
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```
In the example above, the `sequenceDefinition` defines "consecutive" as having a maximum of 36 hours (2160 minutes) between the end of one shift and the start of the next shift.
More information can be found in [Consecutive shifts worked](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/work-limits/consecutive-shifts-worked).

We’ve implemented a system that reduces the problem complexity for the solver. The solver can now make smarter choices about which employee it assigns, based on:

- 
Required skill coverage: The solver now only assesses employees with the required skills for assignments. 
- 
Required tag coverage. The solver now only assesses employees for shifts when they have the required tags. 
- 
Prohibited employees. The solver doesn’t assess prohibited employees for shifts they are prohibited from working. 

Before, the solver had to test all of these cases by evaluating solutions. Now the solver knows not to spend time choosing employees that do not fit these cases. This makes the solver more efficient, so it can reach better solutions in less time.

Data pipelines that submit schedules often need to detect and handle validation issues automatically. Until now, validation messages were human-readable strings that were difficult to parse programmatically.

The endpoint `GET /v1/schedules/{id}/validation-result` now returns structured validation issues that your code can act on directly.
Each issue includes a machine-readable `code` (e.g. `EMPLOYEE_REQUIRED_TAGS_IGNORED`), a `severity` (`ERROR` or `WARNING`), and potentially more properties that identify the affected entity, such as the shift or employee that caused the issue.

This makes it possible to build automated mitigations.

Two related endpoints let you discover all supported issue types:

- 
`GET /v1/schedules/validation-issue-types`lists every issue type the model can produce.
- 
`GET /v1/schedules/validation-issue-types/{code}`returns details for a specific issue type.

If you define a [planning window](https://docs.timefold.ai/user-guide/input-datasets/planning-window), constraint matches whose shifts all end before the planning window start are now skipped, both in constraint violations and in metrics.

For example, with a planning window starting on 1st July 2026, a [Daily shift pairing](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/shift-rotations-and-patterns/daily-shift-pairings#_daily_shift_pairings) between two April 2026 shifts is no longer evaluated.

This makes reporting more targeted and improves the model’s performance.

We have fixed a bug in daily shift pairing rules that caused the pairing to be incorrectly satisfied for same-day pairing (`dayOffset` set to 0).

Constraint weights are now capped at 1,000,000,000,000 (one trillion).
The limit prevents score overflow and nonsensical optimization results that can occur when weights are set too high.
It is enforced when saving a configuration profile and when submitting a dataset.
For more information, see [constraint weights](https://docs.timefold.ai/user-guide/constraints#constraintWeights).

Employee pairings now support a `commonTagType` field, making it possible to enforce that paired employees work shifts that share the same tag of a given category.

This is useful in scenarios where employees not only need to work together but must also cover the same location, route, or department. For example, employees who share a car can now work shifts on the same route, so one employee doesn’t drive to Location A while the other covers Location B.

The pairing type determines the employee’s role in the group:

- 
Employees who declare the pairing through `requiredPairings`require other members to be present.
- 
Employees who declare the pairing through `preferredPairings`can be assigned but prefer working with the other members.

`minutesBetweenShiftsRules` and `minimizeGapsBetweenShiftsRules` now support `excludePreviousShiftTags` and `excludeNextShiftTags`, giving you more flexibility when defining which shift pairs a rule applies to.
Previously you could only specify tags that a shift must have.
Now you can also specify tags that a shift must not have, making it easier to target or skip specific shift types without having to tag every case explicitly.

For example, to enforce a rest period between any two consecutive shifts unless the next shift is a "On-call" shift:

```
{
  "minutesBetweenShiftsRules": [
    {
      "id": "Min12HoursBetweenShifts",
      "minimumMinutesBetweenShifts": 720,
      "excludeNextShiftTags": ["On-call"],
      "shiftTagMatches": "ANY",
      "satisfiability": "REQUIRED"
    }
  ]
}
```
The existing `requiredPriorShiftTags` and `requiredAfterShiftTags` fields have been deprecated and replaced by `includePreviousShiftTags` and `includeNextShiftTags` for consistency.
Similarly, `minimumConsecutivePriorShifts` has been deprecated in favor of `minConsecutivePreviousShifts`.

For more information, see:

The model can now generate shifts from demand curves and shift templates. When shift generation is enabled, the shifts are automatically created as a part of the scheduling workflow. The feature can operate with different shift durations and start times to provide flexibility for scenarios like overtime.

| This is a preview API that may change in future releases. | 

Instead of manually creating individual shifts, add `shiftGeneration` to a `minimumMaximumShiftsPerHourlyDemand` rule with shift templates.

For example, to generate morning and afternoon shifts for an ICU ward that needs two nurses in the morning and three in the afternoon:

```
{
  "minimumMaximumShiftsPerHourlyDemand": [
    {
      "id": "icu-demand",
      "includeShiftTags": ["ICU"],
      "demandDetails": [
        {
          "startDateTime": "2027-02-02T06:00:00Z",
          "endDateTime": "2027-02-02T14:00:00Z",
          "maxDemand": 2
        },
        {
          "startDateTime": "2027-02-02T14:00:00Z",
          "endDateTime": "2027-02-02T22:00:00Z",
          "maxDemand": 3
        }
      ],
      "shiftGeneration": {
        "templates": [
          {
            "id": "morning-8h",
            "baseStartTime": "06:00",
            "baseDuration": "PT8H"
          },
          {
            "id": "afternoon-8h",
            "baseStartTime": "14:00",
            "baseDuration": "PT8H"
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}
```
We introduced new output metrics
`demandGeneratedShifts`, `coveredDemandPersonSlots`, and `uncoveredDemandPersonSlots` to verify the generation result.

The order in which tags and tag types are defined in the input no longer matters. For example, the following input is now valid, even though the tag "Emergency" is defined before its tag type "ShiftType":

```
{
  "modelInput": {
    "tagTypes": [
      {
        "id": "ShiftType"
      }
    ],
    "tags": [
      {
        "id": "Emergency",
        "tagType": "Location"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
This fix makes uploading datasets easier.

Contracts now support `consecutiveShiftsWorkedRules`, which allow you to limit how many shifts employees work consecutively.
The `sequenceDefinition` configuration determines which shifts are consecutive.
Additionally, we support defining conditions for these rules so they are activated in specific cases.

```
{
  "contracts": [
    {
      "id": "NightShiftContract",
      "consecutiveShiftsWorkedRules": [
        {
          "id": "MaxConsecutiveNightShifts",
          "maximum": 5,
          "satisfiability": "REQUIRED",
          "sequenceDefinition": {
            "type": "MAX_MINUTES_BETWEEN_SHIFTS_STARTS",
            "triggerLimit": 2160
          },
          "condition": {
            "type": "MIN_SHIFTS_WORKED",
            "triggerLimit": 2,
            "includeShiftTags": [
              "Night"
            ]
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```
In the example above, the `MaxConsecutiveNightShifts` rule is triggered when an employee works two night shifts (shifts with the "Night" tag).
Once triggered, the rule limits the employee to a maximum of 5 consecutive shifts.
The `sequenceDefinition` defines "consecutive" as having a maximum of 36 hours (2160 minutes) between the start of each shift.

This feature is useful for managing employee fatigue and ensuring compliance with labor regulations regarding consecutive work periods, especially for demanding shifts like night shifts.

Employees can now require or prefer combinations of shift tags, for example "must work in Emergency AND either Wing East or Wing West".
Previously, shift tags on employees could only be listed individually.
With the new `requiredShiftTagsExpression` and `preferredShiftTagsExpression` fields on employees, tags can be combined using AND/OR logic to express richer scheduling requirements.

We replaced the four fixed priority levels (LOW, NORMAL, HIGH, CRITICAL) with a 10-1 numeric scale. This allows for a more granular approach to priority setting, giving you more control over which employees are prioritized. Where 10 is the lowest priority and 1 is the highest priority.

This new way of defining priority allows for more granularity.

[Hourly demand rules](https://docs.timefold.ai/shift-service-constraints/demand-based-scheduling) now allow you to define demand intervals of variable length.
For example, a single demand detail can now span 9:00–17:00 to express a full-day staffing requirement.
You can now express your staffing requirements in a more concise way.

This is enabled by the optional `endDateTime` field on `HourlyDemandDetail`, which now accepts intervals of 30 minutes or longer.
Before, only intervals with length of one hour were supported.
If omitted, the interval defaults to one hour, preserving backward compatibility.

Penalties for over-staffed and under-staffed periods are now more accurate, reflecting the actual length of time the demand is not met.

Disruption rules with `satisfiability: "PREFERRED"` can now also have a `scope` configuration.
Previously, only `REQUIRED` disruption rules supported scopes.

Disruption rules with a preferred satisfiability minimize disruption for employees by assigning shifts that overlap with their original shifts as much as possible.

For example, the following contract defines a PREFERRED disruption rule with an overlap scope:

```
{
  "contracts": [
    {
      "id": "DisruptionContract",
      "disruptionRules": [
        {
          "id": "MinimizeDisruption",
          "satisfiability": "PREFERRED",
          "scope": {
            "scopeType": "OVERLAP"
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```
The weight of the constraint can be adjusted via `minimizePreferredScopedDisruptionForEmployeeWeight` in the config overrides.

When employees have [preferred shift tags](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/shift-type-diversity/shift-tag-types#_preferred_shift_tags), such as a preferred work location or division,
the solver now rewards tag matches more strongly for higher-priority employees.

This allows you to ensure that higher-priority employees are more likely to be assigned to shifts that match their preferred tags, improving employee satisfaction and retention.

By default, breaks are not counted toward hours worked. It is now possible to optionally supply tags for breaks, which specify whether breaks are counted or not towards hours worked for a certain rule.

When `unloggedBreakTags` are specified in a rule, only breaks which match the tags are not counted towards working time. All other breaks are counted for working time.
When no `unloggedBreakTags` are specified in a rule, all breaks will not count towards working time.
For example, you can exclude lunch breaks from working time, but include tea breaks, or similar.

The following rules now accept `unloggedBreakTags`:

You can now specify a scope on disruption rules defined in employee contracts. This scope defines which shifts are deemed disrupted. For example, whether a new shift overlaps with an originally assigned shift, or whether it starts and ends within a certain number of minutes from an original shift’s start and end. This can help with employee retention and well-being as changes are kept to a minimum. This is an experimental API that may change in future releases.

In the example below, if the `new` shift is assigned instead of the `original` shift, then no disruption will be counted,
because the `new` shift starts within 30 minutes of the `original` shift, which is within the rule’s start scope.
The `new` shift also ends 60 minutes before the `original` shift, which is within the rule’s end scope.

```
{
  "modelInput": {
    "employees": [
      {
        "id": "Ann",
        "contracts": [
          "DisruptionContract"
        ]
      }
    ],
    "shifts": [
      {
        "id": "Original",
        "start": "2027-02-01T09:00:00Z",
        "end": "2027-02-01T17:00:00Z",
        "priority": "10",
        "employee": "Ann"
      },
      {
        "id": "New",
        "start": "2027-02-01T09:30:00Z",
        "end": "2027-02-01T16:00:00Z",
        "priority": "1"
      }
    ],
    "contracts": [
      {
        "id": "DisruptionContract",
        "disruptionRules": [
          {
            "id": "DisruptionWithScope",
            "satisfiability": "REQUIRED",
            "scope": {
                "scopeType": "START_AND_END",
                "startScopeInMinutes": 30,
                "endScopeInMinutes": 60
             }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
There are multiple kinds of "scope", such as "START_AND_END" scope and "OVERLAP" scope.
For more information, see [Scope configuration](https://docs.timefold.ai/real-time-planning#_scope_configuration).

This disruption configuration allows you to define a scope around the original start and end times, allowing for minor changes in the schedule without triggering disruption rules.

The model now allows you to specify a total minimum consecutive minutes off for a rolling window.
This total minimum works together with the `consecutiveMinutesOffMinIntervals`.
This makes it possible to specify the employee has, for example, either:

- 
One period of at least 72 consecutive hours off. 
- 
Multiple periods of at least 32 consecutive hours off that add up to at least 72 hours off. 

This is configured using the new `totalConsecutiveMinutesOffMin`:

```
{
  "modelInput": {
    "contracts": [
      {
        "id": "ConsecutiveMinutesOffContract",
        "rollingWindowRules": [
          {
            "id": "Total72hOffMin32hIntervals",
            "rollingWindow": {
              "type": "WEEKLY",
              "size": 1
            },
            "consecutiveMinutesOffLimit":
            {
              "consecutiveMinutesOffMinIntervals": [
                {
                  "count": 3,
                  "consecutiveMinutesOffMin": 1920
                }
              ],
              "totalConsecutiveMinutesOffMin": 4320
            },
            "satisfiability": "REQUIRED"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
This feature allows you to create complex consecutive minutes off requirements by defining consecutive minutes off intervals and a total minimum.

It is now possible to add weights for employee preferred and unpreferred timespans.
This is useful when employees have a number of ranked preferences simultaneously, where one preference is more important than another.
It can also be used to specify that one employee is of a higher priority when fulfilling preferences than another, by giving them a higher weight.
The weight for each timespan is fully customizable.
More information can be found in [Employee preferred times, ranked](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/employee-availability-and-preferences/employee-preferences#_employee_preferred_times_ranked).

You can now minimize disruption individually for each employee. This is configured using the new `disruptionRules` field in employee contracts.
This is useful when the penalty for disrupting some employees is worse than for others, or when some employees have a penalty for disruption and some do not.

Disruption is tracked by two separate constraints:

- 
`Minimize outgoing disruption per employee`: penalizes when an employee loses shifts that were originally assigned to them.
- 
`Minimize incoming disruption per employee`: penalizes when an employee receives shifts that were not originally assigned to them.

Each constraint has its own configurable weight (`minimizeOutgoingDisruptionForEmployeeWeight` and `minimizeIncomingDisruptionForEmployeeWeight`), allowing you to independently control the importance of disruptions for employees losing shifts or gain shifts during replanning.

The `disruptionRules` field of the `globalRules` has been deprecated in favor of the contract-level `disruptionRules`.

Employee pairing has been extended to include tags. Employees can now be paired based on their ID or based on their tags.

```
{
  "employees": [
    {
      "id": "Ann",
      "preferredPairings": [
        {
          "includeEmployeeWithTags": [
            "support"
          ]
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "Beth",
      "tags": [ "support" ]
    }
  ]
}
```
This feature comes in handy when multiple people would be a good fit for pairing with a specific employee. For instance, a new employee Ann needs support whenever they get stuck. All employees with the tag "support" satisfy this requirement.

We have extended shifts to be able to define breaks. These breaks occur during the shift and don’t count towards the time worked. For example, if an employee can only eight hours a day and is assigned a nine-hour shift, then this will be penalized unless the shift has a break of at least one hour.

```
{
  "modelInput": {
    "shifts": [
      {
        "id": "Mon",
        "start": "2027-02-01T08:00:00Z",
        "end": "2027-02-01T17:00:00Z",
        "breaks": [
          {
            "start": "2027-02-01T12:00:00Z",
            "end": "2027-02-01T13:00:00Z"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
For a more in-depth explanation and examples, see:

This feature can be useful if you have breaks during a shift that don’t count towards the time worked.

The model now allows you to specify multiple time off minimums for a single rolling window. For example, an employee must have two intervals of minimum eight consecutive hours off every seven days (7 * 24h).

This is configured using the new `consecutiveMinutesOffMinIntervals`:

```
{
  "modelInput": {
    "contracts": [
      {
        "id": "FullTimeContract",
        "rollingWindowRules": [
          {
            "id": "2xMin8hoursOff",
            "rollingWindow": {
              "type": "WEEKLY",
              "size": 1
            },
            "consecutiveMinutesOffLimit": {
              "consecutiveMinutesOffMinIntervals": [
                {
                  "count": 2,
                  "consecutiveMinutesOffMin": 480
                }
              ]
            }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
This feature makes it easier to define multiple consecutive minute off limits for one rolling window.

We have extended rolling windows support to include conditional requirements. For instance, rolling windows can now be configured to specify an employee can work at most five shifts in a rolling window, if two of those shifts are night shifts. This makes it possible to include conditions for specific times of day, shifts, and weekends and can be applied to time worked and time off.

```
{
  "modelInput": {
    "contracts": [
      {
        "id": "ConditionalRollingWindowRulesContract",
        "rollingWindowRules": [
          {
            "id": "Max36hIf2xNightShift",
            "rollingWindow": {
              "type": "WEEKLY",
              "size": 1
            },
            "minutesWorkedLimit": {
              "minutesWorkedMax": 2160
            },
            "condition": {
              "triggerLimit": 2,
              "type": "MIN_SHIFTS_WORKED",
              "includeShiftTags": ["night shift"]
            }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
Rolling window rules can now be applied conditionally. The rule is evaluated only when a separate trigger condition is met. This works on every rolling window rule type:

For example, an employee can be limited to working at most one weekend in a rolling window only when they have already worked three night shifts in that window.

A new guide, [Configuring employee well-being](https://docs.timefold.ai/scenarios/configuring-employee-wellbeing), was added to the documentation.
This guide provides an overview of well-being optimization constraints and scheduling workflow tools that help you build schedules that are fair, stable, and supportive of employee preferences and work-life balance.

It includes an overview of core well-being concerns (like fairness, rest, rotations, and time-off) with links to the relevant constraints and features.

We have added new input metrics to distinguish between standalone shifts and shift groups:

- 
`standaloneShifts`: The number of shifts not part of any shift group.
- 
`standalonePinnedShifts`: The number of pinned shifts not part of any shift group.
- 
`standaloneMandatoryShifts`: The number of mandatory shifts not part of any shift group.
- 
`standaloneOptionalShifts`: The number of optional shifts not part of any shift group.
- 
`shiftGroups`: The number of shift groups in the input dataset.
- 
`shiftGroupShifts`: The number of shifts that are part of a shift group

Use these metrics to understand the composition of the input data, particularly when combining standalone shifts and shift groups where multiple shifts represent alternatives and only one should be assigned.

The new metrics are only available when shift groups are used in the input dataset.

We have added a new section in the [cost management guide](https://docs.timefold.ai/shift-service-constraints/cost-management/cost-groups#_minimizing_overall_cost) that describes how to configure the model to minimize the overall cost of the schedule.

This is useful when the goal is to minimize labor costs rather than staying within a specific budget range.

We have fixed issues in the rotation periods schema that caused problems when generating clients from the OpenAPI specification.

We have removed the `employeeActivationCost` from the [cost rules](https://docs.timefold.ai/shift-service-constraints/cost-management/cost-management) total cost calculation.
Previously, the activation cost was incorrectly added to every shift assigned to an employee, rather than being applied as a one-time cost when the employee is first activated.

To make it easier to move from what a property does to how and why to use it, the OpenAPI specification and UI now include direct links to the relevant feature guide documentation for key scheduling properties. This helps you transition seamlessly from the technical specification to practical guidance, examples, and best practices when configuring your model.

You can now count only the portion of a shift that overlaps with a specific daily time window toward minutes worked limits. This allows you to express rules such as "maximum 38 hours between 00:00 and 06:00 in every 14 days".

This is configured using the new `countOnlyBetween` field and can be applied to:

This feature is useful for limiting hours worked during specific times of day, such as night shifts or other sensitive time ranges, without affecting the overall minutes worked calculation for other periods.

We have added cost definitions to period rules. These cost definitions can be used to calculate the cost of employees, based on their time worked.
These cost definitions determine how many minutes a person can work at a base rate, and how much time work costs after this base limit is exceeded.
More information can be found in the [cost management documentation](https://docs.timefold.ai/shift-service-constraints/cost-management/employee-rates#_define_employee_rates).

This new feature makes it easy to define the cost of employees, automatically minimizes the cost, and provides useful insights such as the `costDefinitionTotalCost` and `costDefinitionTotalOvertime` output metrics for every employee.

We have added two new fields to the `shift` object;

- 
`requiredSkillsExpression`
- 
`preferredSkillsExpression`

These fields allow a more granular definition for required or preferred skills, such as:

`"Nurse" AND ("ICU" OR "Anesthesia")`
These fields make it easy to define complex skill requirements for shifts.

The logged time for a shift can now be longer than the shift itself for occasions when employees work longer than planned.

We have extended our weekend constraints support with the ability to assign weekend work in rolling windows.

The [Weekends worked in rolling window not in preferred range for employee](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/work-limits/weekends-worked-in-a-rolling-window#_preferred_weekends_worked_in_a_rolling_window)
constraint now allows you to also set a minimum number of weekends an employee has to work within a rolling window. For example, you can now express rules such as:

- 
Minimum 2 weekends worked in any 4-week rolling window 
- 
Minimum 4 weekends worked in any 16-week rolling window 

This complements our existing weekend constraints, making it easier to set up rules to assign weekend shifts.

We have added a warning when we detect `preferredShiftTags` or `requiredShiftTags` on employees and no `shiftTagMatchRule` in the global rules.
This warning indicates that the preferred and required shifts will be ignored if no `shiftTagMatchRules` are present.

We have improved the way we handle duplicate ids. Runs now fail more cleanly if duplicate ids are detected. The example input below will now be handled more cleanly and return an error when submitted.

```
{
  "modelInput": {
    "contracts": [
      {
        "id": "ContractWithDuplicateIds",
        "periodRules": [
          {
            "id": "PeriodRule1"
          },
          {

          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
We have added more granularity to the hourly demand rules, by adding 3 new fields:
`includeEmployeeTags`, `excludeEmployeeTags` and `employeeTagMatches`. These fields can be used to set an hourly
demand for certain employees, by inclusion or exclusion based on tags.

The new fields provide more control over setting demands based on employee availability.

We have added employee output metrics to provide more insights into solutions. This is an experimental API that may change in future releases.

The schedule output now contains a new `employees` section with the following metrics for each employee:

- 
`assignedShifts`: The number of shifts assigned to the employee.
- 
`durationWorked`: The total duration of all shifts assigned to the employee.
- 
`durationOfTimePreferencesMet`: The total duration of preferences met for the employee.
- 
`durationOfTimeUnpreferencesViolated`: The total duration of unpreferences violated for the employee.
- 
`disruptedShifts`: The number of shifts disrupted for the employee.
- 
`durationOfDisruptedShifts`: The total duration of disrupted shifts for the employee.
- 
`overtimeThresholdDuration`: Estimated overtime threshold duration for the employee (derived from weekly period rules). Any duration worked beyond this threshold is considered overtime.
- 
`overtimeWorked`: Estimated total overtime worked (derived from weekly period rules).
- 
`maximumAvailabilityDuration`: Estimated maximum availability duration for the employee (derived from weekly period rules).

The new employee output metrics provide more granular insights into how each employee is scheduled, helping to identify workload distribution, preference satisfaction, and potential overtime issues.

We have fixed a bug where shift priorities with different assignment types couldn’t define the same weight.
Now two shift priorities can have an identical weight as long as one is `MANDATORY` and the other is `OPTIONAL`.

We have removed the need to specify a `maxEmployeeToShiftTravelDistanceInMeters` or `minMinutesBetweenShiftsInDifferentLocations` in the travel configurations to activate the `Minimize Travel Time` constraint.
When an empty `travelConfiguration` is supplied, the constraint will be activated. Note that providing an ID is still required.

We have added two new constraints to manage the number of consecutive weekends employees do not work.

These constraints help enforce restrictions on weekend work, which is important for maintaining employee work-life balance. With these constraints you can set a minimum of consecutive weekends an employee doesn’t work.

We have updated the optional shifts output metric to no longer be present in the output metrics if there are no optional shifts in the input.

We have improved the validation of the model:

- 
Enforced start/end time checks and improved OpenAPI documentation for rules and objects with validity intervals (for example, rule validity). 
- 
Fixed rolling window rule validation so unknown properties are rejected rather than ignored. 
- 
Increased the validation coverage of the model to include edge cases that prevented the model from assigning shifts. These edge cases now trigger warnings so they can be identified but don’t break backwards compatibility. 

These changes help users catch and fix invalid datasets before solving.

We have added support for [flexible skill matching](https://docs.timefold.ai/shift-service-constraints/skills-and-risk-factors#_skill_matching_strategies) through the shift’s `requiredSkillsMatchKind` and `preferredSkillsMatchKind` fields. Two strategies are now available:

- 
`MATCH_ALL`(default): Employee must have all specified skills to be assigned to a shift
- 
`MATCH_ANY`: Employee needs only one of the specified skills to be eligible for a shift

This feature provides greater flexibility in workforce scheduling, especially useful when:

- 
Multiple skill sets can accomplish the same task 
- 
You need to expand the pool of eligible employees for hard-to-fill shifts 

We have added new constraints for optimizing employee activation and managing workforce costs through [Employee activation](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/employee-activation) features:

- 
[Minimize activated employees](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/employee-activation#_minimize_activated_employees): Reduces the number of employees needed by applying activation costs.
- 
[Maximize activated employee saturation](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/employee-activation#_maximize_activated_employee_saturation): Maximizes utilization of activated employees before activating additional staff.
- 
[Keep employee activation ratio](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/employee-activation#_keep_employee_activation_ratio): Maintains the desired proportions between different employee groups (e.g., regular staff vs contractors).

This feature helps reduce labor costs by minimizing the number of employees needed while ensuring optimal utilization of activated staff and maintaining workforce composition requirements.

We have fixed a bug that caused the output metrics calculation not to be calculated correctly when no employees were provided.

We have added support for defining custom shift rotations. Compared to existing weekly rotations, the custom rotations allow for flexibility in the rotation period length.

This feature can help formulate rotation periods such as:

- 
Minimum 14 days of morning, or afternoon shifts 
- 
Maximum 30 days of morning, or afternoon shifts 

We have improved the capabilities of the [Consecutive days worked](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/work-limits/consecutive-days-worked#_consecutive_days_worked) rules to support the definition of [shift sequences](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/work-limits/consecutive-days-worked-and-shift-sequences#_defining_shift_sequences).

A sequence is formed by multiple shifts of the same type, for example morning shifts, not interrupted by other shift types, such as afternoon shifts.

This feature can help formulate use cases such as:

When submitting a schedule with already assigned employees, the `disruption` KPI is now always calculated.
Before, this `disruption` KPI was only calculated when `disruptionRules` were provided.

We have updated penalties for the following constraints to no longer include the shift’s duration in the penalty:

This change makes sure the solver does not treat shifts with different durations as more or less preferred than others.

We have added support for full-time equivalent (FTE) configuration in employee contracts, enabling fair scheduling for employees with different employment types:

This feature allows you to define part-time, full-time, and other employment arrangements while ensuring fair distribution of work. The balance time worked constraint now automatically adjusts for different FTE levels, so a part-time employee (FTE 0.5) working 20 hours is considered equivalent to a full-time employee (FTE 1.0) working 40 hours.

We have extended our weekend constraints support with the ability to limit weekend work in rolling windows:

These constraints allow you to limit the number of weekends an employee can work within a rolling window. For example, you can now express rules such as:

- 
Maximum 2 weekends worked in any 4-week rolling window 
- 
Maximum 4 weekends worked in any 16-week rolling window 

This complements our existing weekend constraints for fixed periods, giving you more options for creating employee-friendly schedules.

We have added support for weekend-related constraints, allowing you to limit weekend work for employees:

These constraints help enforce restrictions on weekend work, which is important for maintaining employee work-life balance. You can:

- 
Limit the total minutes an employee works during weekends in a period 
- 
Limit the number of weekends an employee works in a period 
- 
Limit the number of consecutive weekends an employee works 

Additionally, each contract can define its own weekend configuration, allowing you to customize which days are considered weekend days (by default, Saturday and Sunday).

We have added a new BASIC demo data set which demonstrates a minimal set of Timefold features. This is a simple example that is not meant to be reflective of real-world scheduling needs. It is intended for those early on in their Timefold journey to help them understand the basic features and progress to the more complex features in our other demo data sets.

We have added support for defining hourly rolling window periods for the following rules. Previously, the rolling window rules were only available for daily and weekly periods.

This feature can help formulate constraints that need to be satisfied over a rolling window of time, for example:

- 
Maximum 5 days worked in any 168-hour period 
- 
Maximum 2 night shifts worked in any 168-hour period 
- 
Minimum 2 consecutive days off in any 168-hour period 

We have added a new constraint to rotate shift types for employees.

Use this to make sure that the employee’s shift types rotate in consecutive periods, for example, "morning" shifts on week 1 and "evening" shifts on week 2.

We have introduced 2 new constraints for better handling of consecutive days off.

This feature allows a minimum of consecutive number of days off per period to be set on contracts. So when an employee needs 2 consecutive days off, their contract can define 1 period rule defining "consecutiveDaysOffLimit.consecutiveDaysOffMin: 2".

We have added a new constraint that limits the variation in shift start times. It checks whether the time between the earliest shift start and the latest shift start in this period is larger than the period rule’s shiftStartTimeDifferenceInMinutesMax.

This constraint allows you to assign shifts with similar start times to employees, limiting the range of start times individual employees will have during a specific period of time and reducing the disruption to their daily schedule.

We have added 2 new metrics to provide more insights into solutions.

- 
Assigned shift groups 
- 
Unassigned shift groups 

This update adds metrics that will give more insights into the model output, including how many shift groups were and how many weren’t allocated in the schedule.

A series of updates have been made to the available demo datasets:

- 
The BASIC demo dataset has been removed in favor of the CONTRACT_RULES dataset 
- 
The CONTRACT_RULES demo dataset has been extended to a full week (7 days, 60 shifts) for 13 employees 

This is to better demonstrate the full capabilities of Timefold. The demo data is now more representative of real working rules, including contract patterns, maximum hours worked per day, maximum hours worked per week, preferences, and unavailabilities.

When submitting a new schedule with *unspecified* `unimprovedSpentLimit` in the [run termination configuration](https://docs.timefold.ai/timefold-platform/latest/how-tos/configuration-parameters-and-profiles#_run_termination_settings), the run will use the new diminished returns termination.

Diminished returns terminates the solver early if expected improvements are minimal, saving on CPU costs.
This termination is desirable since it terminates based on the relative rate of improvement, and behaves similarly on different hardware and different problem instances.
You can find more details in the [documentation](https://docs.timefold.ai/timefold-solver/latest/optimization-algorithms/overview#diminishedReturnsTermination).

We have introduced 2 new constraints for better handling of days off.

This feature allows a minimum and/or maximum of days off per period to be set on contracts. This means inputs don’t require the inverse logic with period rules anymore, e.g. when an employee needs 2 days off their contract can define 1 period rule defining "daysOffLimit.daysOffMin: 2", instead of a period rule defining "daysWorkedMax: periodLength - 2" for every period with a different length that the rule would apply to.

We have introduced rolling window rules to define constraints that need to apply over consecutive number of hours, days, or weeks:

This feature can help formulate constraints that need to be satisfied over a rolling window of time, for example:

- 
Maximum 10 Sunday shifts worked in any 52-week period 
- 
Maximum 40 hours worked in any 7-day period 
- 
Minimum 11 consecutive hours off in any 24-hour period 

We have introduced 2 new constraints to limit the number of unique tags that can be used to assign shifts to employees:

This feature can help limit the maximum number of unique tags that can be used to assign shifts to employees. For instance, shift types, routes, skills.

When submitting a recommendations API request, you can specify an optional boolean `includeJustifications` query parameter to control whether constraint match justifications should be included in the response.

This is useful for getting more fine-grained information about the constraint matches, for instance to learn which period rule is violated by the recommended employee assignment.

Priorities have been added to contracts. This means some contracts can now have higher priority than others. By default, the highest priority is "1" and the lowest priority is "10". They respectively have the weights: 10 and 1. This means that a contract with priority "1" will have 10 times the impact of an identical contract with priority "10".

This feature allows for granular control over how much contracts comparatively weigh in solutions. It comes in handy when there is a contract that defines a certain rule that is more important than another, e.g. Contract A defines periodRules which are more important than Contract B’s minutesBetweenShiftRules. In this example, we can set Contract A’s priority to 5 and Contract B’s priority to 10 (default).

When shifts spanned multiple days, counting the days over which the shift spanned wasn’t accurate for periods longer than 1 day and when using the `periodShiftOverlapKind` `START_AND_END`. This is now fixed.

This fix makes sure that shifts spanning multiple days will be accurately counted when using contract period rules with days worked per period and `periodShiftOverlapKind` set to `START_AND_END`.

We have added 4 new KPIs to provide more insights into solutions.

- 
Activated employees 
- 
Total mandatory shifts scheduled 
- 
Total optional shifts scheduled 
- 
Total travel distance 

See OpenAPI Spec or the Timefold Platform UI for a description of their meaning.

This update adds KPIs that will give more insights into the model output, including how many employees were assigned shifts in the schedule, the number mandatory and optional shifts that were scheduled, and the total travel distance.

We have improved the performance and scalability of global rules.

The impacted constraints are:

This improvement will result in finding solutions quicker, especially for large datasets.

A minimum with a `REQUIRED` satisfiability is now deprecated because it may be the cause of infeasible solutions when there is a lack of shifts in the input.
Use the minimum with a `PREFERRED` satisfiability instead.

The impacted constraints are:

This update will result in fewer infeasible solutions when using minimums in the listed constraints.

We have added 3 new input metrics that provide information on the dataset input:

- 
number of employees 
- 
number of shifts 
- 
number of pinned shifts 

See OpenAPI Spec for a description of their meaning.

The Cost Rules, Period Rules, and Global Period Rules previously only checked whether a shift broke a rule if the shift started within the rule’s validity period.
Now this behavior can be configured to also compare the shift’s end time with the rule’s validity period.
See [costs per period not in required range](https://docs.timefold.ai/shift-service-constraints/cost-management/cost-groups#_keep_costs_within_budget)
and [costs per period not in preferred range](https://docs.timefold.ai/shift-service-constraints/cost-management/cost-groups#_preferably_keep_costs_within_a_range) and the [Shift type diversity](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/shift-type-diversity/shift-type-diversity)

We have added a new [concurrent shifts worked not in required range](https://docs.timefold.ai/shift-service-constraints/shift-assignments/shift-selection#_concurrent_shift_rules) constraint to control the maximum number of shifts that can take place at the same time.
The feature is useful in scenarios where the shifts use a shared resource with limited capacity.

It is now possible to specify a list of travel configurations per contract.
Each travel configuration can limit the distance from the home location to a shift’s location and the time between two shifts at different locations, within a certain time period.
See [Shift travel and locations](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/shift-travel-and-locations) for examples.

Contract period rules can now specify minimum and maximum [Minutes logged per period](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/work-limits/minutes-logged-per-period).
This feature can be useful when limiting minimum/maximum shift hours that differ from the scheduled shift start to end interval, e.g. because breaks are not included in the shift working hours.

We have added a new required shift group assignment mode not met constraint to specify the way the [Alternative shifts](https://docs.timefold.ai/shift-service-constraints/alternative-shifts) are assigned within shift groups.
The feature is useful in scenarios where a piece of work (e.g. product demonstration) should only be done once, but we have multiple time slots (shifts) available for it.

We have added a custom move to facilitate matching of `PREFERRED` patterns.

You may also specify the weight of a single-day shift pattern in the relation to the other single-day patterns.
See [Employee works preferred single-day shift sequence pattern](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/shift-rotations-and-patterns/single-day-shift-sequence-patterns#_preferred_single_day_shift_sequence_patterns) rule for more information.

The `REQUIRED` single-day patterns are now deprecated and will be removed in a future version in favor of `PREFERRED` patterns with a high weight.

Single Day Shift Patterns now have a property `ordered` (`true` by default). When set to false, the pattern can be matched even if the shifts don’t follow the same order as their respective pattern elements.

In Employee Contracts, you can specify the minimum or maximum time between shifts with `minutesBetweenShiftsRules`.
You can now provide a scope for these rules.
The scope will limit which pairs of shifts the rule is applied to.
The scope excludes shift pairs where the start of the later shift is after the end of the prior shift plus the scope duration.
See the updated [Shift type diversity](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/shift-type-diversity/shift-type-diversity) for examples.

We have extended shift priorities to distinguish between `mandatory` (default) and `optional` shifts.
Optional shifts are useful in scenarios when conformance with a soft constraint (e.g. a `PREFERRED` multi-day pattern rule) is more desired than having an extra shift assigned.

We have added a custom move to facilitate matching of `PREFERRED` patterns.

We have added 4 new KPIs that provide information on the employees' preferences:

- 
Average Duration of Employees' Preferences Met 
- 
Minimum Duration of Preferences Met Across Employees 
- 
Average Duration Employee’s Unpreferences are Violated 
- 
Maximum Duration of Unpreferences Violated Across Employees 

See OpenAPI Spec or the Timefold Platform UI for a description of their meaning. These KPIs are marked as experimental and subject to change. We would love your feedback.

We have fixed the multi-day pattern rules to correctly handle a pattern starting with `OFF`.
If you use a pattern starting or ending with `OFF`, you must specify the [planning window](https://docs.timefold.ai/user-guide/input-datasets/planning-window) interval to ensure the pattern matches properly throughout the whole period you are planning for.

The `REQUIRED` multi-day patterns are now deprecated and will be removed in a future version in favor of `PREFERRED` patterns with a high weight.

We have replaced the existing demo datasets with new ones that are more realistic and better showcase the model’s features.

The new demo datasets cover basic Employee Shift Scheduling capabilities, Contract Period Rules, and Hourly Demand Rules.

We have added the ability to define custom priorities and weights for shifts. Whenever the model needs to choose between multiple shifts to assign to an employee, it will favor shifts with higher priority.

We are renaming the "Employee Scheduling" model to "Employee Shift Scheduling" to distinguish between future other models involving scheduling for employees. (We are not changing API urls or entity names, because …)

Use this rule to make sure the time worked is balanced fairly across employees.

Tags can now be used to define preferred and required shifts for employees.

See documentation of the rules for more information:

All ISO 8601 local date time types have been replaced by ISO 8601 local date time with offset to UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) to support multiple time zones.

Employees and shifts can now provide a location. This allows you to restrict the possible shifts where an employee can work and minimize the travel distance.

# Getting started: Hello world

The Employee Shift Scheduling model assigns shifts to employees with the goals of creating schedules that minimize labor costs, ensure proper shift coverage, and treat employees fairly and with respect.

This guide introduces Timefold’s Employee Shift Scheduling model and walks you through the steps to use Timefold Platform to create an optimized Employee Shift Scheduling solution.

To follow the steps in this guide, you need to be registered on Timefold Platform and have access to an active tenant.

## Request a trial

- 
Navigate to [https://app.timefold.ai](https://app.timefold.ai).
- 
Click Log in. 
- 
Click Sign up. Either enter the email address and password you want to register with and click continue or select one of the federated log-in options and follow the prompts. 
- 
Verify your email address. 
- 
Click **Request a trial**.

A member of our team will contact you to arrange a trial.

The steps in this guide can be completed in under 10 minutes:

This hello world example uses an example with 1 employee and 1 shift to demonstrate the process of requesting and retrieving a solution from Timefold’s Employee Shift Scheduling model.

At the end of this guide, you will have a solution for the Employee Shift Scheduling hello world problem.


A dataset for the Employee Shift Scheduling model must include information about your shifts and your employees' availability.

The following is an example Employee Shift Scheduling input dataset:

```
{
  "config": {
    "run": {
      "name": "Hello world example"
    }
  },
  "modelInput": {
    "employees": [
      {
        "id": "Beth"
      }
    ],
    "shifts": [
      {
        "id": "Mon",
        "start": "2027-02-01T00:00:00Z",
        "end": "2027-02-01T08:00:00Z"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
| Copy this example dataset into a file called `sample.json`to use in this hello world example. | 

The `modelInput` object of the dataset contains the data to be optimized.

At a minimum, `modelInput` must include `employees` and `shifts`:

In this example, there is 1 {supply}.
`employees` must include an `id`.

- 
`id`is a unique identifier that identifies the individual employee.

```
{
  "employees": [
    {
      "id": "Beth"
    }
  ]
}
```
In this example, there is 1 {DEMAND}.
`{demand}` includes an `id`, `start`, and `end`.

- 
`id`is a unique identifier that identifies the individual shift.
- 
`start`is the start time of the shift in[ISO 8601 date and time format](https://www.iso.org/iso-8601-date-and-time-format.html).
- 
`end`is the end time of the shift in[ISO 8601 date and time format](https://www.iso.org/iso-8601-date-and-time-format.html).

```
{
  "shifts": [
    {
      "id": "Mon",
      "start": "2027-02-01T00:00:00Z",
      "end": "2027-02-01T08:00:00Z"
    }
  ]
}
```
You have two options to post the dataset.

Typically, you post the dataset to the API. However, for testing purposes, you can upload your `sample.json` file directly in the Timefold Platform UI:

- 
Log into the Timefold Platform dashboard: [https://app.timefold.ai](https://app.timefold.ai)
- 
Select the Employee Shift Scheduling tile. 
- 
Click **New plan**.
- 
Select **Custom**and click**Next**
- 
Upload the `sample.json`file you saved earlier.
- 
Click **Next**, then click**Run**.

You need an API key to access the API.

## Learn how to configure an API Key to run the examples in this guide:

- 
Log in to Timefold Platform: [app.timefold.ai](https://app.timefold.ai/).
- 
From the **Dashboard**, click your**tenant**, and from the drop-down menu select**Manage tenant**, then choose**API Keys**.
- 
Create a new API key or use an existing one. Ensure the list of models for the API key contains the current model. 

In the examples, replace `<API_KEY>` with the API Key you just copied.

POST the dataset contained in the `sample.json` file for solving to the API endpoint: [https://app.timefold.ai/api/models/employee-scheduling/v1/schedules](https://app.timefold.ai/api/models/employee-scheduling/v1/schedules)

```
The output includes an `ID` that has been assigned to the dataset.
You’ll use this `ID` to retrieve the solution for your dataset.

`solverStatus` confirms the dataset has been scheduled for solving.

Append the `<ID>` from the output you received to the endpoint [https://app.timefold.ai/api/models/employee-scheduling/v1/schedules](https://app.timefold.ai/api/models/employee-scheduling/v1/schedules)

`curl -X GET -H 'X-API-KEY: <API_KEY>' https://app.timefold.ai/api/models/employee-scheduling/v1/schedules/<ID>````

# Introduction

Source: https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-shift-scheduling/latest/introduction.html

# Introduction

The Employee Shift Scheduling model is one of the Scheduling APIs available on the [Timefold Platform](https://app.timefold.ai/).

The Employee Shift Scheduling model assigns shifts to employees with the goals of creating schedules that minimize labor costs, ensure proper shift coverage, and treat employees fairly and with respect.

The model runs on the [Timefold Platform](https://docs.timefold.ai/timefold-platform/latest) and the application includes [Timefold Enterprise Solver](https://docs.timefold.ai/timefold-solver/latest/enterprise-edition/enterprise-edition), a scalable optimization engine that can solve complex constraint satisfaction problems.

The Employee Shift Scheduling model includes constraints for:

- 
Matching employee availability, skills, and preferences with shifts. 
- 
Complying with labor law and regulations. 
- 
Scheduling priority shifts. 
- 
Managing shift rotations and patterns. 
- 
Keeping shift assignments within budget. 

To learn more about individual constraints, see the [Employee resource constraints](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/employee-resource-constraints) and [Shift service constraints](https://docs.timefold.ai/shift-service-constraints/shift-service-constraints) guides.

[Constraints](https://docs.timefold.ai/user-guide/constraints) have configurable weights, making them adjustable to meet different business goals and priorities.

The [real-time planning](https://docs.timefold.ai/real-time-planning) API makes plans adaptable when unforeseen events inevitably occur, and the [recommendations](https://docs.timefold.ai/recommendations) API can help you figure out which employees to assign to which shifts.

The REST API layer is defined on top of the model and serves as a communication point with the engine to provide a stable interface that allows you to manage the lifecycle of the optimization problem, from submitting the initial dataset to retrieving the final solution.

Backend developers, integration engineers, full-stack developers, and technical consultants implement the model in an application or workflow.

# Manual intervention

Source: https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-shift-scheduling/latest/manual-intervention.html

# Manual intervention

Different industries have different scheduling requirements and it isn’t always possible to automatically assign and optimize every shift.

In employee shift scheduling you can pin one or many shifts when a specific employee or group of employees must be assigned to specific shifts.

Even after you’ve implemented fully automated and optimize scheduling, there are still times when it is necessary to manually intervene and assign specific shifts manually.

Shifts are pinned by setting `pinned` to `true` for the shift and adding the employee ID of the employee who has been assigned to the shift to `employee`:

```
{
  "shifts": [
    {
      "id": "Mon A1",
      "start": "2027-02-01T09:00:00Z",
      "end": "2027-02-01T17:00:00Z",
      "pinned": true,
      "employee": "Ann"
    },
    {
      "id": "Dinner 1",
      "start": "2027-02-01T09:00:00Z",
      "end": "2027-02-01T17:00:00Z",
      "pinned": true,
      "employee": "Beth"
    }
  ]
}
```
Pinning is useful in the following scenarios:

When you first start evaluating scheduling options it can be useful to compare the outcome of different solutions. This could mean comparing a solely human generated schedule with a schedule generated by Timefold or comparing solutions between Timefold and another company.

In order for any comparison to be useful it must use the same data and apply the same constraints.

To compare a schedule from Timefold with an existing schedule from a human planner or another scheduling solver, create an input dataset with the shifts and employees that were scheduled by the human planner or the other solver, and pin every shift with the employee the shift was assigned to:

```
{
  "id": "Shift Mon 1",
  "start": "2027-02-01T09:00:00Z",
  "end": "2027-02-01T17:00:00Z",
  "pinned": true,
  "employee": "Ann"
}
```
To generate a schedule from Timefold, create a copy of the dataset from the previous step and unpin all the shifts by removing `"pinned": true,` and the employee:

```
{
  "id": "Shift Mon 1",
  "start": "2027-02-01T09:00:00Z",
  "end": "2027-02-01T17:00:00Z"
}
```
Add the [contractual constraints](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/employee-contracts) that must be considered, for instance, employees work 8 hours a day for a total of 40 hours per week:

```
{
  "contracts": [
    {
      "id": "fullTimeContract",
      "periodRules": [
        {
          "id": "Max8HoursPerDay",
          "period": "DAY",
          "satisfiability": "REQUIRED",
          "minutesWorkedLimit": {
            "minutesWorkedMax": 480
          }
        },
        {
          "id": "Max40HoursPerWeek",
          "period": "WEEK",
          "satisfiability": "REQUIRED",
          "minutesWorkedLimit": {
            "minutesWorkedMax": 2400
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```
```
{
  "employees": [
    {
      "id": "Carl",
      "availableTimeSpans": [
        {
          "start": "2027-02-02T00:00:00Z",
          "end": "2027-02-06T00:00:00Z"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```
In Timefold Platform create plans for both the comparison dataset and Timefold dataset.

Timefold will respect the pinned shifts in the comparison dataset and create an optimized schedule for the Timefold dataset. Both plans will be assigned a score, the higher the score, the better the quality of the schedule.

Both plans will include output metrics that can give you a sense of how the plans compare. These include:

- 
Assigned shifts 
- 
Unassigned shifts 
- 
Activated employees 

Complex technology is rarely adopted all at once.

With pinning you can gradually introduce Timefold into the scheduling process as you build trust in the plans it generates.
This also gives you time to fine-tune the [constraints and constraint weights](https://docs.timefold.ai/user-guide/constraints) that are used in your datasets.

To gradually adopt Timefold, decide on which portion of the schedule Timefold will optimize (perhaps starting with one region or business function) and gradually increase over time.

Real-time planning makes it possible to change schedule even when the schedule is being executed, for instance, to assign new employees to shifts, due to sick leave or additional demand. You can use pinning in real-time planning to minimize the disruption caused by the re-planning process.

Self-rostering lets employees choose or express preferences for the shifts they work. Pinning is the primary tool for honoring guaranteed self-rostered choices: when an employee’s selection is confirmed, pin the shift to that employee so the optimizer treats the assignment as fixed. For non-guaranteed selections, soft preferences give the optimizer the flexibility to assign a different employee when needed.

Combining self-rostering with optimization requires careful configuration to balance employee
autonomy with coverage and fairness goals.
See [Self-rostering and optimization](https://docs.timefold.ai/scenarios/self-rostering-and-optimization) for a
full guide, including best practices and a real-world case study.

When employees have the flexibility to choose one shift they want to work (a joker shift), this shift is pinned to the employee to ensure it is assigned to them and isn’t assigned to another employee.

# Real-time planning with patches

Source: https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-shift-scheduling/latest/real-time-planning-preview.html

# Real-time planning with patches

| This guide describes features currently available as a preview feature.
If you’d like early access to this feature, please [Contact us](https://timefold.ai/contact).
For information about the current supported feature, see[Real-time planning](https://docs.timefold.ai/real-time-planning). | 

Employee shift schedules are typically published a few weeks in advance to allow employees to plan the rest of their lives around the shifts they’ll be working.

This means employees don’t need to organize things (social events, appointments, child care, life administration) at the last minute which reduces stress and improves their job satisfaction.

However, even the best schedule can be disrupted at the last minute by employees calling in sick or a sudden need for additional staff.

Real-time planning makes it possible to assign new employees to shifts, due to sick leave or additional demand, and to minimize the disruption caused by the re-planning process.

This guide explains real-time planning with the following examples:

| ## Learn how to configure an API Key to run the examples in this guide:
 In the examples, replace  |

- 
1 person from 16:00 to 20:00 to set up, take early orders, and cover the busy period. 
- 
2 people from 17:00 to 21:00 to cover the busy period. 
- 
1 person from 18:00 to 22:00 to cover the busy period, help pack up, and prepare for the following day.

Unfortunately, Carl has called in sick for his shift, so the schedule needs to be regenerated.

The input dataset can be modified and re-solved to create a revision of the plan by creating and submitting a patch.

Carl is sick so his availability is no longer accurate and `availableTimeSpans` for the day should be removed.

- 
Input 
- 
Patch

  "path": "/employees/[id=Carl]/availableTimeSpans/0"
}

It’s not always possible (or even preferable) to pin every existing shift when real-time planning is necessary, however, you can minimize the disruption real-time planning causes with a global configuration rule.

```
{
  "globalRules": {
    "disruptionRules": [
      {
        "id": "minimizeDisruptionShortTerm",
        "start": "2027-02-01",
        "end": "2027-02-02",
        "multiplier": 1
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
`disruptionRules` must include an `id`, and `start` and `end` times that specify when the rule is applied.

Any disruption to the schedule will invoke the `Employee assignment disrupted on replanning` soft constraint and impact the soft score of the final solution, which incentivizes Timefold to minimize the disruption.

| This rule is more likely to be satisfied for employees with a higher employee priority.
See [Employee priority](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/employee-priority)for more details. | 

| Every soft constraint has a weight that can be configured to change the relative importance of the constraint compared to other constraints. | 

A `multiplier` can also be included, which multiplies the soft score by the multiplier.
The multiplier can be between 1 and 5 inclusive.

Multiple disruption rules can be configured with different multipliers to give extra weight to shifts happening sooner in the schedule:

```
{
  "globalRules": {
    "disruptionRules": [
      {
        "id": "minimizeDisruptionShortTerm",
        "start": "2027-02-01",
        "end": "2027-02-07",
        "multiplier": 5
      },
      {
        "id": "minimizeDisruptionLongTerm",
        "start": "2027-02-08",
        "end": "2027-02-14",
        "multiplier": 1
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
| This rule is more likely to be satisfied for employees with a higher employee priority.
See [Employee priority](https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-resource-constraints/employee-priority)for more details. | 

In the following example, Ann, Beth, Carl, and Dan are assigned shifts in the restaurant, but Carl calls in sick.
This time, instead of pinning Ann’s, Beth’s, and Dan’s shifts, the employees who were originally assigned to the shifts are added to the shift, `pinned` is set to false (or omitted altogether), Carl is unavailable, and a disruption rule is applied.

The output includes the `disruptionPercentage` KPI which shows 25% of the shifts were disrupted due to the change.

A shift can be considered replanned when its employee changes during replanning, so if the shift gets unassigned or assigned to another employee. By default, a replanned shift is also considered disrupted.

The scope field can prevent shifts from being considered disrupted.
The type of scope is defined by the `scopeType`.

| When rules define scope, they don’t trigger the constraints to minimize incoming and outgoing disruption. Those constraints are triggerd for rules without scopes defined. | 

| This is an experimental API subject to change. There are no guarantees on backward compatibility. | 

Disruption rules with a scope can either have a `REQUIRED` or a `PREFERRED` satisfiability.
If the satisfiability is `REQUIRED`, then any shift that falls within the scope of the disruption rule will not be considered disrupted.
If the satisfiability is `PREFERRED`, then Timefold will try to maximize the overlap between the replanned shifts and the original shifts.

When using a `START_AND_END` scope type, you must define two fields:

- 
`startScopeInMinutes`: The number of minutes around the original start time within which the new shift must start to count as non-disruptive.
- 
`endScopeInMinutes`: The number of minutes around the original end time within which the new shift must end to count as non-disruptive.

If a replanned shift starts and ends within these scopes of an original shift, it isn’t considered a disrupted shift.
For example, if an employee was originally assigned to a shift from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM, and the replanned shift has a `startScopeInMinutes` of 30 minutes and an `endScopeInMinutes` of 0 minutes, the new shift will be considered:

- 
Not disrupted, if it starts between 8:30 AM and 9:30AM and ends at 5:00PM. 
- 
Disrupted, in any other case. 

This configuration allows you to define a buffer around the original start and end times, allowing for minor changes in the schedule without triggering disruption rules.

```
{
  "modelInput": {
    "employees": [
      {
        "id": "ann",
        "contracts": [
          "disruptionContract"
        ]
      }
    ],
    "shifts": [
      {
        "id": "original",
        "start": "2027-02-01T09:00:00Z",
        "end": "2027-02-01T17:00:00Z",
        "priority": "10",
        "employee": "ann"
      },
      {
        "id": "new",
        "start": "2027-02-01T09:05:00Z",
        "end": "2027-02-01T17:00:00Z",
        "priority": "1"
      }
    ],
    "contracts": [
      {
        "id": "disruptionContract",
        "disruptionRules": [
          {
            "id": "disruptionWithScope",
            "satisfiability": "REQUIRED",
            "scope": {
                "scopeType": "START_AND_END",
                "startScopeInMinutes": 30,
                "endScopeInMinutes": 0
             }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
In the example above, the new shift with the higher priority will be assigned. It won’t count as disrupted because it starts and ends within the scopes of the original shift’s start and end times.

If the satisfiability is `PREFERRED`, then Timefold will try to maximize the overlap between the replanned shifts and the original shifts.
For example, an employee was originally assigned to a shift from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM, and the scope has a `startScopeInMinutes` of 30 minutes and an `endScopeInMinutes` of 30 minutes. There are two shifts that are candidates for assignment:

- 
Shift A starts at 8:45 AM and ends at 4:45 PM. 
- 
Shift B starts at 9:30 AM and ends at 5:30 PM. 

In this case, Shift A is assigned because it has more overlap with the original shift.

When using an `OVERLAP` scope type, no further configuration is required.

If a replanned shift overlaps with an original shift, it’s not considered a disrupted shift.

```
{
  "modelInput": {
    "employees": [
      {
        "id": "ann",
        "contracts": [
          "disruptionContract"
        ]
      }
    ],
    "shifts": [
      {
        "id": "original",
        "start": "2027-02-01T09:00:00Z",
        "end": "2027-02-01T17:00:00Z",
        "priority": "10",
        "employee": "ann"
      },
      {
        "id": "new urgent shift",
        "start": "2027-02-01T09:30:00Z",
        "end": "2027-02-01T17:30:00Z",
        "priority": "1"
      }
    ],
    "contracts": [
      {
        "id": "disruptionContract",
        "disruptionRules": [
          {
            "id": "disruptionWithScope",
            "satisfiability": "REQUIRED",
            "scope": {
                "scopeType": "OVERLAP"
             }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
In the example above, the new shift with the higher priority will be assigned. It won’t count as disrupted because it overlaps with the original shift.

If the satisfiability is `PREFERRED`, then Timefold will try to maximize the overlap between the replanned shifts and the original shifts.
This means that the shift or combination of shifts with the largest overlap with the original shift will be assigned.
For example, an employee was originally assigned to a shift from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM, and the overlap scope is active. There are three shifts that are candidates for assignment:

- 
Shift A starts at 8:00 AM and ends at 3:00 PM. 
- 
Shift B starts at 9:00 AM and ends at 12:00 PM. 
- 
Shift C starts at 1:00 PM and ends at 5:00 PM. 

In this case, Timefold assigns both Shift B and Shift C because together they have more overlap with the original shift, even though Shift A has more overlap with the original shift than either Shift B or Shift C.

In some industries it is important to have employees on standby (or on call) who can step in to take over a shift if another employee is suddenly unavailable. Real-time planning can take advantage of this kind of backup planning.

Shifts can be assigned different priorities, where 1 is the highest priority and 10 is the lowest:

```
{
  "shifts": [
    {
      "id": "2027-02-01-icu-1",
      "start": "2027-02-01T08:00:00Z",
      "end": "2027-02-01T16:00:00Z",
      "priority": "1"
    },
    {
      "id": "2027-02-01-icu-2",
      "start": "2027-02-01T08:00:00Z",
      "end": "2027-02-01T16:00:00Z",
      "priority": "1"
    },
    {
      "id": "2027-02-01-icu-3",
      "start": "2027-02-01T08:00:00Z",
      "end": "2027-02-01T16:00:00Z",
      "priority": "1"
    },
    {
      "id": "2027-02-01-icu-on-call",
      "start": "2027-02-01T08:00:00Z",
      "end": "2027-02-01T16:00:00Z",
      "priority": "5"
    }
  ]
}
```
If there are enough employees, 3 will be assigned to the high priority shifts, and 1 will be assigned to the lower priority on-call shift. If one of the 3 employees assigned to the high priority shifts calls in sick, the on-call employee will be ready to step in and take their place.

# Real-time planning

Source: https://docs.timefold.ai/employee-shift-scheduling/latest/real-time-planning.html

# Real-time planning

Employee shift schedules are typically published a few weeks in advance to allow employees to plan the rest of their lives around the shifts they’ll be working.

This means employees don’t need to organize things (social events, appointments, child care, life administration) at the last minute which reduces stress and improves their job satisfaction.

However, even the best schedule can be disrupted at the last minute by employees calling in sick or a sudden need for additional staff.

Real-time planning makes it possible to assign new employees to shifts, due to sick leave or additional demand, and to minimize the disruption caused by the re-planning process.

This guide explains real-time planning with the following examples:

| ## Learn how to configure an API Key to run the examples in this guide:

- 
1 person from 16:00 to 20:00 to set up, take early orders, and cover the busy period. 
- 
2 people from 17:00 to 21:00 to cover the busy period. 
- 
1 person from 18:00 to 22:00 to cover the busy period, help pack up, and prepare for the following day.
